qs.q: A patient with chronic heart failure develops hypertension, tachycardia, raised jugular venous pressure, and peripheral oedema halfway through a red blood cell transfusion. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop the transfusion and administer IV furosemide
Administer packed red cells alongside fluid boluses
Stop the transfusion and administer IV adrenaline
Continue the transfusion slowly while giving oxygen
qs.e: This patient is experiencing Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload, which presents with hypertension and signs of volume overload requiring cessation of transfusion and loop diuretics. Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis, not hydrostatic pulmonary oedema.

faq.a: Early effusion may not yet impede right‑atrial filling; the pressure rise appears only when the fluid volume exceeds the pericardial reserve.
faq.q: Why can JVP be normal in early cardiac tamponade?

faq.a: Pressing on the liver for 10 seconds should raise the JVP >3 cm in right‑sided failure; a negative test suggests normal right‑sided pressure.
faq.q: What is the hepato‑jugular reflux test?

faq.a: Severe malaria can cause myocardial depression and fluid overload, leading to secondary right‑sided congestion and raised JVP.

exam: A 28‑year‑old with penetrating chest injury presents with hypotension, clear lungs and JVP 5 cm above the sternal angle – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Cardiac tamponade; perform emergency pericardiocentesis.
In a patient with HIV, TB pericarditis is suspected. Which bedside sign differentiates tamponade from constrictive pericarditis? — Pulsus paradoxus present in tamponade, absent in constriction.

A patient with acute chest pain and raised JVP has an ECG without ST‑elevation. What condition should you consider and what test confirms it? — Right‑ventricular infarction; bedside echocardiography showing RV dilation.
Why is aggressive diuresis harmful in right‑ventricular infarction with raised JVP? — It reduces preload, worsening RV output and systemic hypotension.
How would you assess JVP in an obese patient where neck veins are not visible? — Use lateral neck view, measure vertical distance from the clavicle, and perform hepato‑jugular reflux.

A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops new raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. What complication should you suspect and what is the next step? — Drug‑induced pericardial effusion/tamponade; arrange urgent pericardiocentesis.

What feature on bedside ultrasound distinguishes massive pulmonary embolism from tamponade? — RV free‑wall hypokinesis with preserved pericardial space versus pericardial fluid with diastolic RV collapse.

Explain why low voltage QRS on ECG supports a diagnosis of tamponade rather than RV infarction. — Fluid dampens electrical signals, producing low voltage; RV infarction typically shows ST changes, not low voltage.
ai.title: Raised Jugular Venous Pressure
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Raised JVP is a bedside sign of elevated right‑sided filling pressures. It helps differentiate cardiac tamponade, right‑ventricular infarction and other causes of systemic venous congestion, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Measure with patient supine, head turned 45° left
Use the sternal angle as zero point
3 cm above the sternal angle = raised
sections.p: Jugular venous pressure (JVP) is the height of the venous column in the internal jugular vein when the patient is at 30‑45° head elevation. It is considered raised when the vertical distance from the sternal angle exceeds 3 cm.

b: 0: not visible
1: <3 cm above sternal angle
sections.p: Clinical grading (0‑5) correlates with central venous pressure (CVP).

b: Cardiac tamponade (trauma, pericardial TB, malignancy)
Right‑ventricular myocardial infarction
Constrictive pericarditis (often TB)
Severe tricuspid regurgitation (rheumatic heart disease, carcinoid)
Pulmonary embolism
Severe chronic lung disease (COPD, bronchiectasis)
Advanced heart failure (ischemic, hypertensive, sickle‑cell cardiomyopathy)
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the commonest causes are conditions that raise right‑heart filling pressure.

b: Neck vein pulsation visible above clavicle
Prominent ‘a‑wave’ in tamponade or RV infarction
Clear lungs in isolated right‑sided congestion
Crackles if left‑sided failure co‑exists
sections.p: Patients may be dyspnoeic, hypotensive, or have peripheral oedema. The neck veins are visibly distended, often with a prominent ‘a‑wave’ in tamponade.

t.b: Is there pericardial fluid or RV collapse? → Fluid suggests tamponade; RV collapse confirms it.
Is there ST‑elevation in V1‑V4 or low voltage? → ST‑elevation points to RV infarction; low voltage suggests pericardial effusion.
Is the cardiac silhouette enlarged? → Enlarged silhouette supports tamponade or massive effusion.
Is it raised? → Supports myocardial infarction; normal in isolated tamponade.
Positive? → TB pericarditis is a common cause of tamponade in the region.

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable, perform percussion of the liver and assess hepato‑jugular reflux
t.b: Positive reflux indicates elevated right‑sided pressure.

b: Systolic BP <90 mmHg with clear lungs
Muffled heart sounds (Beck’s triad)
Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg
Sudden worsening of JVP with chest pain
sections.p: Unrecognised tamponade or massive RV infarction can cause rapid circulatory collapse.

b: Cardiac tamponade – urgent pericardiocentesis (needle) or surgical drainage; avoid NSAIDs that may worsen TB pericarditis.
RV infarction – give aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation; avoid excessive diuretics that reduce preload.
Constrictive TB pericarditis – start anti‑TB therapy + steroids; avoid high‑dose diuretics early.
Severe tricuspid regurgitation – diuretics for congestion, consider valve surgery when feasible.
Pulmonary embolism – give anticoagulation (heparin) if not contraindicated; avoid thrombolysis if active bleeding.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support venous return and oxygenation.

b: Repeat bedside ultrasound to confirm fluid resolution
Monitor for recurrent effusion in TB pericarditis
Educate patients on early reporting of chest trauma or dyspnoea
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce secondary cardiac stress
sections.p: Re‑assess JVP after each intervention; arrange definitive care for chronic causes.

b: Carotid artery pulsation – felt laterally, not mid‑neck, and has a single upstroke.
Thyroid goitre – non‑pulsatile, moves with swallowing.
Cervical lymphadenopathy – firm, non‑pulsatile, not height‑dependent.
sections.p: Distinguish raised JVP from other neck swellings.

b: Obesity can hide JVP; use lateral neck view.
Low‑output states may blunt the ‘a‑wave’ even in tamponade.
Chest X‑ray may appear normal early in tamponade.
sections.p: Certain bedside signs may be absent despite serious pathology.

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic BP <90 mmHg with raised JVP
Muffled heart sounds or pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg
